reference.source: Tachdjian's Pediatric Orthopaedics / Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: A traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle rather than a true osteonecrosis
Affected site is the tibial tuberosity at the insertion of the patellar tendon
Typically affects athletic adolescents, roughly ten to fifteen years, and is more common in boys, often bilaterally
Presents with anterior knee pain and a tender, sometimes prominent, swollen tibial tubercle aggravated by running, jumping and kneeling
The radiographic hallmark is fragmentation and irregularity of the tibial tubercle with overlying soft-tissue swelling
Pain is reproduced by resisted knee extension and by direct pressure over the tuberosity
A residual bony ossicle or prominent tubercle may persist into adulthood and occasionally remain symptomatic
Management is conservative with activity modification, quadriceps and hamstring stretching, and physiotherapy, with surgery reserved for a persistent painful ossicle as needed
reference.pathophysiology: Osgood-Schlatter disease is a traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity, the apophysis onto which the patellar tendon inserts. Repetitive, forceful quadriceps contraction during running and jumping transmits tension through the patellar tendon to the developing tuberosity at a time when the apophysis is still partly cartilaginous and mechanically weak. This repeated microtrauma causes small avulsive injuries, inflammation and heterotopic ossification within the distal patellar tendon and apophysis, producing the characteristic prominence and fragmentation. Rapid adolescent growth, with relative tightness of the extensor mechanism, increases the traction load. The condition typically settles as the tuberosity ossifies and the apophysis fuses, although a separate ossicle can persist and remain a source of pain.
additionalDifferentials: Bone tumour or infection of the proximal tibia
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination reproducing pain over the tibial tubercle with resisted extension
Lateral knee radiographs to assess tubercle fragmentation and exclude other lesions
Ultrasound to evaluate the distal patellar tendon and any ossicle or bursitis
Magnetic resonance imaging in atypical or persistent cases
Assessment of extensor mechanism flexibility and lower limb alignment
Inflammatory markers if infection or inflammatory arthropathy is suspected
redFlags: Acute severe pain and inability to extend the knee suggesting a tibial tubercle avulsion fracture
Rest pain, night pain or systemic symptoms raising concern for infection or malignancy
A rapidly enlarging mass or lytic bony change on imaging
Persistent disabling pain after skeletal maturity indicating a symptomatic ununited ossicle
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is favourable; symptoms are self-limiting and usually resolve as the tubercle ossifies and the apophysis fuses, though a prominent tubercle or persistent ossicle may cause residual discomfort with kneeling in a minority of patients.
pitfalls: Overlooking an acute tibial tubercle avulsion fracture in an adolescent presenting with sudden severe pain
Confusing the condition with Sinding-Larsen-Johansson syndrome at the inferior patellar pole
Failing to address extensor mechanism tightness that perpetuates apophyseal traction
Recommending prolonged complete rest rather than graded activity modification
